lines: IT WAS NEVER TRYING TO BE.

ACT_1.secondary: At or below 2,000 pounds, to sell for no more than $2,000. A vice president conceived the project and was its moving force.

ACT_1.quote: Pinto, however, was a rush project, so that styling preceded engineering and dictated engineering design to a greater degree than usual. Among the engineering decisions dictated by styling was the placement of the fuel tank.
ACT_1.attribution: Grimshaw v. Ford Motor Co., 119 Cal. App. 3d 757 (1981)

ACT_1.quote: A design decision was made to place the fuel tank behind the rear axle rather than above that axle. A primary reason for this decision was that if the fuel tank were located above the axle the Pinto would have been left with a very small trunk.
ACT_1.attribution: Gary T. Schwartz, “The Myth of the Ford Pinto Case”, 43 Rutgers L. Rev. 1013 (1991), at 1015

items.label: The opinion — “9 or 10 inches of crush space”

ACT_1.quote: I would say they were all bad.
ACT_1.attribution: A prosecution witness at the Indiana criminal trial, on the bumpers of the Pinto, Gremlin, Vega and Dodge Colt — Schwartz, 43 Rutgers L. Rev. at 1015 n.6

ACT_1.quote: This location, however, was by no means unique to the Pinto; rather, it was a commonplace at the time in American cars.
ACT_1.attribution: Gary T. Schwartz, “The Myth of the Ford Pinto Case”, 43 Rutgers L. Rev. 1013 (1991), at 1027

ACT_1.quote: The crash tests revealed that the Pinto's fuel system as designed could not meet the 20-mile-per-hour proposed standard.
ACT_1.attribution: Grimshaw v. Ford Motor Co., 119 Cal. App. 3d 757 (1981)

ACT_1.primary: 21 MILES PER HOUR, INTO A FIXED BARRIER
ACT_1.secondary: The filler neck torn from the tank; the tank punctured by a bolt head on the differential housing.

ACT_1.primary: NHTSA · INVESTIGATION REPORT PHASE I · C7-38 · MAY 1978
ACT_1.secondary: Office of Defects Investigation. Stamped OFFICIAL USE ONLY; a portion withheld under 5 U.S.C. 552(b)(4).

ACT_1.label: Per car — reinforced rear structure, smooth axle, improved bumper, added crush space. The COURT'S Pinto figure. It is not the $11.

ACT_1.quote: The Pinto crash tests results had been forwarded up the chain of command to the ultimate decision-makers and were known to the Ford officials who decided to go forward with production.
ACT_1.attribution: Grimshaw v. Ford Motor Co., 119 Cal. App. 3d 757 (1981)

ACT_1.secondary: Exhibit 125, “Fuel System integrity Program financial review”, was received and discussed. This document WAS in evidence. The famous 1973 report was not.

ACT_1.quote: A design cost savings $10.9 million (1974-1975) can be realized by this delay.
ACT_1.attribution: Exhibit 125, quoted in Grimshaw v. Ford Motor Co., 119 Cal. App. 3d 757 (1981)

ACT_1.quote: Currently there are no plans for forward models to repackage the fuel tanks.
ACT_1.attribution: Exhibit 125, quoted in Grimshaw v. Ford Motor Co., 119 Cal. App. 3d 757 (1981)

ACT_1.quote: In October 1971, Ford officials decided against incorporating any of these modifications into current Pintos; rather, it would wait until NHTSA clarified its position.
ACT_1.attribution: Gary T. Schwartz, “The Myth of the Ford Pinto Case”, 43 Rutgers L. Rev. 1013 (1991), at 1018

ACT_1.quote: In 1973, NHTSA promulgated its fuel-tank standard but ruled that this standard would apply only to 1977 models.
ACT_1.attribution: Gary T. Schwartz, “The Myth of the Ford Pinto Case”, 43 Rutgers L. Rev. 1013 (1991), at 1018

ACT_2.quote: On May 28, 1972, Mrs. Gray, accompanied by 13-year-old Richard Grimshaw, set out in the Pinto from Anaheim for Barstow to meet Mr. Gray. The Pinto was then 6 months old and had been driven approximately 3,000 miles.
ACT_2.attribution: Grimshaw v. Ford Motor Co., 119 Cal. App. 3d 757 (1981)

ACT_2.quote: It was later established that the carburetor float had become so saturated with gasoline that it suddenly sank, opening the float chamber and causing the engine to flood and stall.
ACT_2.attribution: Grimshaw v. Ford Motor Co., 119 Cal. App. 3d 757 (1981)

ACT_2.primary: THE CLOSING SPEED, AS THE JURY FOUND IT
ACT_2.secondary: “from 50 to 55 miles per hour but before the impact had been braked to a speed of from 28 to 37 miles per hour.”

ACT_2.quote: In fact, Ford's basic position at trial—which the court's opinion at no point mentions—was that the approaching car (a Ford Galaxie) had not slowed down at all, and had struck the Gray car at a speed in excess of 50 miles per hour.
ACT_2.attribution: Gary T. Schwartz, “The Myth of the Ford Pinto Case”, 43 Rutgers L. Rev. 1013 (1991), at 1016 n.9

ACT_2.quote: A 1972 Ford Pinto hatchback automobile unexpectedly stalled on a freeway, erupting into flames when it was rear ended by a car proceeding in the same direction.
ACT_2.attribution: The opening sentence of Grimshaw v. Ford Motor Co., 119 Cal. App. 3d 757 (1981)

ACT_2.quote: Mrs. Gray died a few days later of congestive heart failure as a result of the burns.
ACT_2.attribution: Grimshaw v. Ford Motor Co., 119 Cal. App. 3d 757 (1981)

ACT_2.quote: Because Ford does not contest the amount of compensatory damages awarded to Grimshaw and the Grays, no purpose would be served by further description of the injuries suffered by Grimshaw or the damages sustained by the Grays.
ACT_2.attribution: The court, declining to describe them further — Grimshaw v. Ford Motor Co., 119 Cal. App. 3d 757 (1981)

ACT_2.quote: Plaintiffs settled with the other defendants before and during trial; the case went to verdict only against Ford Motor Company.
ACT_2.attribution: Grimshaw v. Ford Motor Co., 119 Cal. App. 3d 757 (1981)

ACT_2.label: Hours the jury deliberated, after a six-month trial — Schwartz, 43 Rutgers L. Rev. at 1017

ACT_2.quote: The jury actually awarded Grimshaw $2,841,000 compensatory damages and $125 million punitive damages and the Grays $659,680 compensatory damages.
ACT_2.attribution: Grimshaw v. Ford Motor Co., 119 Cal. App. 3d 757 (1981), footnote 1 — what the JURY awarded, not what Ford paid: the punitive award was remitted to $3,500,000

ACT_2.secondary: Judgment modified to $2,516,000 for Grimshaw and $559,680 for the Grays.

ACT_2.quote: The court noted, however, that the amount of the punitive award was 44 times the compensatory award
ACT_2.attribution: The trial court's stated reason, as recited in Grimshaw v. Ford Motor Co., 119 Cal. App. 3d 757 (1981)

ACT_2.quote: or that the jury did utilize Exhibit 125, or any other exhibits, and if they did, that they were justified in so doing.
ACT_2.attribution: The trial judge, expressly declining to say how the jury reached $125,000,000 — a figure he then remitted to $3,500,000. Grimshaw v. Ford Motor Co., 119 Cal. App. 3d 757 (1981)

ACT_2.quote: The Grays' motion to amend their complaint to add allegations seeking punitive damages was denied on the ground such damages are not recoverable in a wrongful death action.
ACT_2.attribution: Grimshaw v. Ford Motor Co., 119 Cal. App. 3d 757 (1981)

ACT_3.secondary: By Mark Dowie. A source for what was published in 1977, and for nothing else.

ACT_3.quote: A Mother Jones Classic: For seven years the Ford Motor Company sold cars in which it knew hundreds of people would needlessly burn to death.
ACT_3.attribution: Mark Dowie, “Pinto Madness”, Mother Jones, September/October 1977 — the standfirst

ACT_3.quote: By conservative estimates Pinto crashes have caused 500 burn deaths to people who would not have been seriously injured if the car had not burst into flames. The figure could be as high as 900.
ACT_3.attribution: Mark Dowie, “Pinto Madness”, Mother Jones, September/October 1977 — no source is given for either number in the retrieved text

ACT_3.quote: Ford waited eight years because its internal “cost-benefit analysis,” which places a dollar value on human life , said it wasn’t profitable to make the changes sooner.
ACT_3.attribution: Mark Dowie, “Pinto Madness”, Mother Jones, September/October 1977 — the stray space before the comma is in the published text

ACT_3.quote: This cost-benefit analysis argued that Ford should not make an $11-per-car improvement that would prevent 180 fiery deaths a year.
ACT_3.attribution: Mark Dowie, “Pinto Madness”, Mother Jones, September/October 1977 — the sentence that became the story

ACT_3.secondary: Mother Jones, edited in San Francisco, launched the article with Mark Dowie accompanied by Ralph Nader.

ACT_3.quote: Following public release of the article, ‘Pinto Madness’, the NHTSA initiated, on August 11, 1977, a preliminary evaluation of the alleged safety defect, and on September 13, a formal defect investigation case.
ACT_3.attribution: NHTSA Office of Defects Investigation, Investigation Report Phase I, C7-38, May 1978, p.2

ACT_3.quote: A test program of staged vehicle-to-vehicle rear-end collisions was developed and a contract awarded for the performance of these tests.
ACT_3.attribution: NHTSA Office of Defects Investigation, Investigation Report Phase I, C7-38, May 1978, p.2

ACT_3.quote: Of the consumer letters and other inquires, only one involved an actual report of a fire occurrence in a Pinto vehicle upon rear-end impact, not previously reported to the NHTSA through other sources.
ACT_3.attribution: NHTSA Office of Defects Investigation, Investigation Report Phase I, C7-38, May 1978, p.3 (“inquires” is the report's own spelling)

items.label: Settled out of court or judgement against Ford
Settled in favor of Ford / under investigation

ACT_3.quote: FARS does not record the cause of death, only its fact; it does not distinguish between deaths due to impact and those caused by the fire.
ACT_3.attribution: NHTSA Office of Defects Investigation, Investigation Report Phase I, C7-38, May 1978, p.10 — the agency's own caveat on its own number

ACT_3.secondary: NHTSA scheduled a hearing for 14 June to enable Ford to reply.

ACT_3.label: Vehicles in NHTSA recall campaign 78V143000, received 19 June 1978 — a longer filler pipe and a polyethylene shield
of Pinto owners responded to the 1978 recall offer — a NHTSA official, by telephone, to Schwartz. Not a document.

ACT_4.quote: BENEFITS AND COSTS RELATING TO FUEL LEAKAGE ASSOCIATED WITH THE STATIC ROLLOVER TEST PORTION OF FMVSS 208
ACT_4.attribution: The caption of the table itself — E. S. Grush & C. S. Saunby, “Fatalities Associated with Crash Induced Fuel Leakage and Fires” (Ford, 1973), p.6

ACT_4.primary: FATALITIES ASSOCIATED WITH CRASH INDUCED FUEL LEAKAGE AND FIRES
ACT_4.secondary: E. S. Grush and C. S. Saunby, Ford Environmental and Safety Engineering, headed “Attachment II”. Not “the Pinto memo”.

ACT_4.quote: The Ford report took the form of an attachment to a submission by Ford to NHTSA, dated September 19, 1973, captioned a Petition for Reconsideration of Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standard No. 301
ACT_4.attribution: Gary T. Schwartz, “The Myth of the Ford Pinto Case”, 43 Rutgers L. Rev. 1013 (1991), at 1020 n.21

ACT_4.quote: The NHTSA has issued Notice 2 of Docket 70-20 and Notice 1 of Docket 73-20, both regarding fuel system integrity.
ACT_4.attribution: E. S. Grush & C. S. Saunby, “Fatalities Associated with Crash Induced Fuel Leakage and Fires” (Ford, 1973), first paragraph, p.1

ACT_4.quote: The analysis discussed below concerns the static rollover requirement proposed for FMVSS 301.
ACT_4.attribution: E. S. Grush & C. S. Saunby, “Fatalities Associated with Crash Induced Fuel Leakage and Fires” (Ford, 1973), p.4 — the Table 3 caption on p.6 says FMVSS 208. The paper contradicts itself and this film says so.

ACT_4.quote: It was the rollover situation, and not the rear-end-impact situation, that was the subject of the Ford document.
ACT_4.attribution: Gary T. Schwartz, “The Myth of the Ford Pinto Case”, 43 Rutgers L. Rev. 1013 (1991), at 1020

ACT_4.quote: Savings - 180 burn deaths, 180 serious burn injuries, 2100 burned vehicles.
ACT_4.attribution: E. S. Grush & C. S. Saunby, “Fatalities Associated with Crash Induced Fuel Leakage and Fires” (Ford, 1973), Table 3, p.6

ACT_4.quote: Unit Cost - $200,000 per death, $67,000 per injury, $700 per vehicle.
ACT_4.attribution: E. S. Grush & C. S. Saunby, “Fatalities Associated with Crash Induced Fuel Leakage and Fires” (Ford, 1973), Table 3, p.6 — total benefit $49.5 million

lines: THE WORD PINTO IS NOT IN THE TABLE.

ACT_4.quote: While these are Ford costs, they have been applied across the industry in this analysis.
ACT_4.attribution: E. S. Grush & C. S. Saunby, “Fatalities Associated with Crash Induced Fuel Leakage and Fires” (Ford, 1973), p.7

ACT_4.quote: The NHTSA estimate of 2000 to 3500 fatalities yearly in fire-involved motor vehicle crashes appears to overstate the seriousness of the fire problem.
ACT_4.attribution: E. S. Grush & C. S. Saunby, “Fatalities Associated with Crash Induced Fuel Leakage and Fires” (Ford, 1973), p.1 — Ford arguing its own case to a regulator, on a sample of 24

ACT_4.quote: the likelihood of a given crash resulting in fuel spillage is much higher for rear impacts (26 percent with spillage in the sample studied) than for other crash types, such as frontals (3.5 percent spillage).
ACT_4.attribution: E. S. Grush & C. S. Saunby, “Fatalities Associated with Crash Induced Fuel Leakage and Fires” (Ford, 1973), p.1

ACT_4.quote: The casualty to dollars conversion factors used in this study were the societal cost values prepared by the NHTSA (6). These values are generally higher than similarly-defined costs from other sources, and their use does not signify that Ford accepts or concurs in the values.
ACT_4.attribution: E. S. Grush & C. S. Saunby, “Fatalities Associated with Crash Induced Fuel Leakage and Fires” (Ford, 1973), p.7 — (6) is the paper’s own footnote marker for NHTSA’s 1972 societal-cost report

ACT_4.quote: The 1973 Ford report can fairly be faulted for not taking account of NHTSA's explanation of the implications of its own figure.
ACT_4.attribution: Gary T. Schwartz, “The Myth of the Ford Pinto Case”, 43 Rutgers L. Rev. 1013 (1991), at 1024 n.41 — Schwartz correcting his own earlier reading

ACT_4.quote: And in a 1972 report the agency decided a human life was worth $200,725.
ACT_4.attribution: Mark Dowie, “Pinto Madness”, Mother Jones, September/October 1977 — two sentences before “Ford has a better idea: $200,000.”

ACT_4.quote: Indeed, a primary reason given by the trial judge in ruling against the admissibility of the Ford report was that Ford was using the figure that NHTSA itself preferred.
ACT_4.attribution: Gary T. Schwartz, “The Myth of the Ford Pinto Case”, 43 Rutgers L. Rev. 1013 (1991), at 1023 n.35

ACT_5.label: Maximum penalties in total — Associated Press, 14 September 1978

ACT_5.primary: THE GRAND JURY CHARGED NO PERSON

Judgment as No. 11-431, Pulaski County Circuit Court

ACT_5.quote: Because the reckless homicide statute had been enacted only in 1977, Ford could not be prosecuted for the reckless design of the Pinto; rather, the prosecution needed to show a reckless post-1977 failure by Ford to repair or warn.
ACT_5.attribution: Gary T. Schwartz, “The Myth of the Ford Pinto Case”, 43 Rutgers L. Rev. 1013 (1991), at 1017

ACT_5.quote: Largely because of the narrowness of the resulting issue, at trial the prosecution was not able to secure the admission of internal Ford documents on which it had hoped to build its case.
ACT_5.attribution: Gary T. Schwartz, “The Myth of the Ford Pinto Case”, 43 Rutgers L. Rev. 1013 (1991), at 1017

ACT_5.secondary: The prosecution said the Pinto was moving. The defence said it was stopped, and that any car of that era would have taken similar damage. — Christian Science Monitor, 14 March 1980

ACT_5.primary: 13 MARCH 1980 — NOT GUILTY, ON ALL COUNTS
ACT_5.secondary: “This case was not appealed from the trial level.” Indiana Law Review 14:1 (1981), n.11 — the word is broken “ap-/pealed” by the scan. There is no state appellate opinion.

ACT_5.quote: In crash-testing, NHTSA compared the Pinto to the Chevrolet Vega, often regarded (along with the Gremlin) as having the least safe gas tank of the other subcompacts for sale in America. In this process, the Pinto consistently flunked tests that the Vega was able to pass.
ACT_5.attribution: Gary T. Schwartz, “The Myth of the Ford Pinto Case”, 43 Rutgers L. Rev. 1013 (1991), at 1028

ACT_5.quote: It further showed, however, that the Pinto's rear-fire fatality rate, while considerably below the Gremlin's, was considerably above the respective rates of the Vega, Toyota, Mazda, and Datsun.
ACT_5.attribution: Ford's own comparative memorandum, described in Gary T. Schwartz, “The Myth of the Ford Pinto Case”, 43 Rutgers L. Rev. 1013 (1991), at 1032 — Ford did not introduce it at its own criminal trial

ACT_5.quote: It is plausible to believe, then, that because of these costs, Ford decided not to improve the Pinto's design, knowing that its decision would increase the chances of the loss of consumer life. Once a variety of misconceptions are stripped away, this limited core of the Pinto story remains.
ACT_5.attribution: Gary T. Schwartz, “The Myth of the Ford Pinto Case”, 43 Rutgers L. Rev. 1013 (1991), at 1034-1035

ENDING.quote: From what I have been able to learn, as for safety the Pinto was a car that was neither admirable nor despicable.
ENDING.attribution: Gary T. Schwartz, “The Myth of the Ford Pinto Case”, 43 Rutgers L. Rev. 1013 (1991), at 1066-1067 — the last words of the film
